title: One Door to Every Mind

post.author: u/night_subs_aoife
post.title: I subtitle films on the night shift, alone. The usage page says our busiest forty minutes every night are my break, when every tool on my screen sits idle. Tonight the meter switched everything off.

blocks.text: I'm Aoife, night subtitle editor at Lowlight Subtitles, a small studio that writes the words you read along the bottom of films. I work 23:00 to 07:40, alone in the building. My break is 01:00 to 01:40.

Four of our tools send work to a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back. A company called a provider runs the model and sells its use. One tool turns speech into text. One translates. One checks our subtitles for timing and spelling. The fourth, the archive summariser, writes notes on every film we've ever done. It runs by itself on an old computer in the back office.

The provider bills by the token, the small pieces of text a model reads and writes. Every message a tool sends carries a key: a long secret code, like a password, that tells the provider which account to bill. Mr Corrigall, who set our tools up, pasted the same key into all four.

Mr Teasdale, the owner, set a spending limit on the account: the most a month may cost, $1,500. He calls it our budget. Once the month's bill reaches it, the provider refuses every message until the 1st, unless he raises it.

The provider's usage page shows what the account spent, in ten-minute bars. It has one line, because we have one key. On a working night each bar is about $0.83: $5 an hour, $40 a night. The summariser runs once a week, on Sundays, Mr Corrigall says, for about $65. September had four Sundays. Its bill was $1,460.

Tonight at 01:40 I came back from my break and started the speech tool. Spending limit reached. The translator said the same, and so did the checker. A feature film's subtitles are due at a broadcaster at 06:00.
This is tonight on the usage page. Each line is one ten-minute bar: when it starts, and what the account spent in it.

I went back through the month. Every night since 1 October has the same four bars, 01:00 to 01:40, $16.25 each. That's my break. The building is empty but for me, and every tool on my screen sits idle. In September those bars came only on Sundays.
The busiest forty minutes of every night are the forty minutes nobody works.
I went to the back office. The old computer was on, its fan humming, its screen locked. I don't have the password. Mr Corrigall is away until tomorrow, and his phone goes to voicemail.

diagram.aria: Aoife's drawing of how the studio's tools reach the provider. Four tools on the left: speech to text, the translator and the checker on her screen, and the archive summariser in the locked back office. All four send their messages with one key, pasted into each. Every message is billed to one provider account, whose usage page has one line and whose limit of $1,500 a month was full at 01:15.

blocks.caption: Drawn tonight. Speech to text, the translator and the checker run on my screen; the archive summariser runs on the old computer in the back office, which I can't open. All four send their messages with the same key, so the provider bills one account and its usage page has one line. The account's limit is $1,500 a month. It was full at 01:15, while I was on my break.

blocks.text: Mr Teasdale says the limit did its job and he'll raise it from his phone. Mr Corrigall once told us bigger studios put a gateway in front of the provider: one program every tool talks to instead, which passes each message on and holds the real key itself. He said we were too small to need one. What should we change, tonight and after?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your studio is haunted, though a meter that runs fastest in an empty room comes close. A provider never sees your building. It sees messages, requests in its own word, each carrying a key, and it bills the account behind that key. So your usage page can only ever have as many lines as you have keys, and tonight one line is all four tools. The program Mr Corrigall described has a name some of you know from The Front Desk on the night shift board: a gateway, one door every request passes through on its way in. Two questions. Of your four tools, which can run when nobody is at a keyboard? And what did 01:00 look like on the last Sunday in September, the Tuesday after it, and the first night of October?

replies.author: u/night_subs_aoife
replies.text: Only the summariser runs by itself. Sunday 27 September: four bars from 01:00, $16.25 each. Tuesday 29 September: nothing at 01:00. Thursday 1 October: the four bars, and every night since. Mr Corrigall told me Sundays when he set it up in August. Nobody here remembers changing anything, and its settings are behind that password.

comments.author: u/ship_it_gallimore
comments.text: The limit did its job. It's a fuse: something drew more than usual, the fuse blew, and nothing worse happened. You have a film due at six. Raise the limit to $3,000 tonight, get the film out, and read the usage page every Monday. A gateway is one more program to run and one more thing to break at 3 AM. Working out which tool spent what is a job for a quiet week, not for 01:45.

replies.author: u/night_subs_aoife
replies.text: Mr Teasdale is saying the same thing on the phone.

replies.author: u/ship_it_gallimore
replies.text: Then he's right twice. Ship the film.

comments.author: u/own_accounts_strachan
comments.text: At my last studio every tool had its own account with the provider: its own key, its own spending limit, its own bill. When one tool ran wild it stopped itself and nobody else. No gateway, nothing extra in the middle to break. The provider already does the counting, so let it.

reply.prompt: The film is due at 06:00 and the account is full at $1,500.00. What should Lowlight change, tonight and after? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise the monthly spending limit so tonight's film ships, and check the usage page weekly.
options.verdict: A bigger fuse, the same dark
options.part2: At 01:40 I rang Mr Teasdale and he raised the limit to $3,000 from his phone. The three tools came straight back, and the film reached the broadcaster before six. On Mondays I read the usage page: the same four bars at 01:00 every night, one line, no names. Mr Corrigall came back and said the summariser runs on Sundays, so nobody opened it. On 29 October the account filled at 07:40, the minute my shift ended. October's bill was $3,000.00, more than twice September's. At 23:00 every tool said spending limit reached, with a documentary due at dawn.
options.senior: A spending limit on the whole account is one fuse for everything. It can tell you that the account spent too much, never which tool did, and when it blows it stops every tool together. Raising it buys tonight and nothing else: the job at 01:00 kept spending $65 a night, so the bigger fuse blew two weeks later. Keep the provider's limit, but as the last fence, set above the sum of per-tool budgets, so it trips only if everything inside has failed. Anthropic's rate-limits page describes this kind of account-wide limit: once usage reaches a limit you set, requests are refused until you raise or remove it.

options.text: Give each tool its own provider account, so one tool's spending can never stop the others.
options.verdict: Four doors, four bills, nobody watching
options.part2: At 01:40 Mr Teasdale opened three new accounts with the provider from his phone, one each for speech, translation and the checker, with limits of $700, $400 and $200, guessed from September's one-line bill, and I pasted the three new keys in. New accounts start on the provider's lowest limits for how many messages may arrive a minute, so the speech tool kept being told too many requests, and the film reached the broadcaster after six. The summariser, still on the old, full account, was refused. The next day Mr Corrigall gave it an account of its own with a $350 limit. At 01:15 on 22 October that account filled and stopped it. Nobody noticed: it showed only on the summariser's own usage page, one of four we now had to read, with four bills. October came to $2,525.00 across five accounts, and nobody could say why the summariser had spent $350 in six nights.
options.senior: Separate accounts do stop one tool's spending from stopping the others; that part is right. But every account is another real key pasted into another machine, another bill and another usage page, so the picture gets more scattered, not clearer. Nothing sits between the tools and the provider, so there is no single place to see all the spending, change a model for every tool, or send translation to a second provider: each of those needs another round of accounts and keys. New accounts can also start small: Anthropic's page says new organizations may start in an Evaluation tier with limits below the standard ones. A gateway gives the same per-tool budgets with one real key, one log and one place to route.

options.text: Put a gateway in front: it holds the real key; each tool gets its own key and budget.
options.part2: At 01:40 Mr Teasdale raised the limit to $2,500 to see October out, and the film reached the broadcaster before six. The next day Mr Corrigall set up a gateway. He made a new real key, kept it only in the gateway, and switched the old one off. Each tool got its own gateway key and a monthly budget: speech $700, translation $400, the checker $200, the summariser $350. On 17 October, a Saturday, the gateway's log showed the summariser's key spending $65.00 between 01:00 and 01:40. Mr Corrigall opened its settings. On 30 September Ms Mirrlees, our day editor, had changed it from weekly to nightly, thinking it was the backup job. At 12:00 it went back to Sundays. October came to $2,435.00, under the $2,500 limit. From November the provider's limit is $1,700, just above the four budgets together, $1,650. Had the gateway been there since September, the summariser's key would have stopped at $350, at 01:15 on 6 October, and my three tools would have run on.
options.senior: Put one program between your tools and every model provider. The real provider keys live only there. Each app gets its own gateway key, which can be switched off without touching the others. Each key carries its own budget in money, and if you like a cap on tokens or requests per minute, so a runaway job stops itself and nothing else. Every request becomes a log line with the key, the model, the tokens and the cost, so the bill splits by tool and a strange pattern has a name on its first night. Because every tool talks to one interface, the gateway can also route by model name: translation to one provider, speech to another, with no change in the tools. LiteLLM's gateway is one open-source example: one endpoint for over a hundred providers, and keys that each carry their models, budgets and rate limits. Keep the provider's own limit as the outer fence, above the sum of the budgets. The cost: one more program to run and protect, which every tool now depends on.

options.text: Make a new key tonight and paste it into every tool I can reach, so the unknown spender stops.
options.verdict: It stops, and nobody learns why
options.part2: At 01:40 Mr Teasdale made a new key from his phone and switched the old one off. I pasted the new key into the three tools on my screen. They were refused anyway: the account had spent $1,500.00 of its $1,500, and a new key doesn't empty it. He raised the limit to $2,500 and the film went out before six. From 01:00 on 16 October the summariser's old key was refused, and the 01:00 bars stopped. Nobody knew why. At 12:00 Mr Corrigall found the summariser failing and pasted the new key into it. From the next night the four bars were back, every night, and at 04:40 on 25 October the account filled again.
options.senior: Switching a key off does stop a spender you can't find, and if a key had leaked it would be the right first move. Here nothing leaked: a job you own was running on a schedule nobody checked. Swapping one shared key for another shared key teaches nobody what the job was, and the next person to mend the failing tool pastes the key back in and brings the job back with it. Note too that a key is not the limit. The limit belongs to the account, so a new key on a full account is still refused. Give each tool its own key, so one can be switched off without the others, and keep a log line per key, so the next strange bar has a name.

sim.title: Read the meter: one key or one door
sim.lede: You're Aoife, reading the provider's meter from 1 September to 31 October. No real model runs here: each tool's spend is stated data. The three tools on her screen (speech to text, the translator, the checker) work during her shift, 23:00 to 07:40 with her break from 01:00 to 01:40: 480 minutes a day, $22, $12 and $6 a day, $40 in all, $5 an hour. The archive summariser runs from 01:00 to 01:40 on its run days, $65 a run, $1.625 a minute: on Sundays, until its schedule was changed on 30 September to every night from 1 October. A bar is ten minutes of spending, as on the usage page. A month counts from 00:00 on the 1st. Every spending limit and budget works like a meter: messages pass while it has room, and from the moment it fills, every later message behind it is refused until the month resets. With one shared key, all four tools sit behind the account's $1,500 limit. With an own account per tool, each account's limit is that tool's budget. With a gateway, each tool gets its own key from the gateway, with its budget, and every message also counts on the one account behind the real key, which only the gateway holds. Days after 15 October are ahead of tonight: what happens if nothing else changes. Play a plan applies a reply from 01:40 tonight, as its Part 2 tells it.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you open on 30 September, the day the schedule changed: September $1,460.00. Inspect 6 October and find the four $16.25 bars from 01:00 to 01:40. Inspect 14 October, $1,470.00, then 15 October: $1,475.00 at 01:00, and all four refused from 01:15. Switch the schedule to weekly all along and watch October end at exactly $1,500.00; then switch it back. Choose the gateway with the summariser's budget at $350: only its key stops, at 01:15 on 6 October, and on the 15th the three tools run on. Set that budget to $250 and even the weekly job stops on 27 September. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing haunted the studio. The archive summariser, changed from weekly to nightly on 30 September, spent $65 at 01:00 every night on the same key as Aoife's three tools, and a usage page with one key can only show one line. On the 15th its run filled the $1,500 limit at 01:15.

steps.title: One key, one line.
steps.text: A provider bills each request in steps. First the tool sends its request with a key. Second the provider looks the key up and finds the account behind it. Third the model reads the input tokens and writes the output tokens. Fourth the provider prices those tokens and adds the cost to that account, under that key. The usage page then adds the costs up by key and by time. It never knew there were four tools, only one key, so all four came out as one line. What can go wrong: a job nobody watches spends on the same line as everyone else, and the only clue is when it spends. Here that was 01:00 to 01:40, $16.25 a bar, every night since 1 October, where September had it only on Sundays.

steps.title: A limit on the account stops every tool at once.
steps.text: The provider keeps a running total for the month. Before each request it compares the total with the limit; once the total reaches the limit, it refuses every request on the account, from any tool, until the month resets or someone raises the limit. In September four weekly runs ($260) and thirty days of work ($1,200) made $1,460. In October the nightly runs made fourteen by the end of the 14th, $910, with $560 of work: $1,470. Midnight to 01:00 on the 15th added $5. The 01:00 run needed only $25 of its $65, and at 01:15 the total reached $1,500. What can go wrong: one job spends everyone's share, and the limit can't say whose. Even with the job weekly, October would have touched $1,500 in its last minute: a limit sized to last month, with no room.

steps.title: A gateway: one door between the tools and every provider.
steps.text: The Front Desk drew an API gateway: a program in front of other programs that checks and routes each request. A gateway for models does the same job with money and tokens. In steps: first a tool sends its request to the gateway, with its own gateway key. Second the gateway checks that key is allowed and has budget left. Third it reads the model name in the request and picks the provider that serves it. Fourth it swaps in the real provider key, which only the gateway holds, and passes the request on. Fifth, when the answer comes back, it writes a log line (key, model, tokens, cost) and adds the cost to that key's spend. What can go wrong: the gateway is now on every request's path, a single point of failure: if it stops, every tool stops, and it holds the keys that matter, so it needs guarding like a safe.

steps.title: A budget per key, in money and in tokens.
steps.text: Each gateway key gets a monthly budget sized from what that tool really needs. The summariser's should cover its busiest honest month: five Sundays, five runs, $325, so about $350. Nightly runs would then fill it on the sixth night, at 01:15 on 6 October, and stop only the summariser. A first guess of $250 is below even four runs ($260) and would have stopped the weekly job on 27 September. Gateways also cap tokens or requests per minute per key, so one burst can't crowd out the rest. Above all the budgets ($700, $400, $200, $350, together $1,650), keep the provider's own limit as an outer fence, $1,700, so it trips only if the gateway fails. What can go wrong: budgets set by guesswork. Read a month of per-key log lines before you fix them.

steps.title: What the gateway costs you.
steps.text: It is one more program to run, update and watch, and the one every tool now waits on: run it on reliable hardware and know what happens when it is down. It can add a little delay to every request. Its log lines can hold what tools sent, so decide what to keep and for how long. And it moves the risk rather than removing it: the real keys sit in one place, which is better than four, but that place must be locked and its own access logged. Build Night X5 builds one: cost and speed through an LLM gateway, with caching and routing on top of the keys and budgets here.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as one door. Four tools on the left each hold their own gateway key with a monthly budget: speech to text $700, the translator $400, the checker $200, the archive summariser $350. All four talk to the gateway, which holds the real key and writes a log line per request. The gateway passes requests to the provider, whose limit of $1,700 sits above the budgets, and could route by model name to a second provider later.

explain.caption: Read left to right. Each tool sends its requests with its own gateway key, and each key has a monthly budget: $700, $400, $200 and $350, $1,650 together. Only the gateway holds the real key; it writes a log line for every request, so the bill splits by tool. The provider's own limit, $1,700, sits above the budgets as the last fence. A second provider can be added later and chosen by model name, with no change in the tools.

fix.title: The fix: one door, a key and a budget per tool, a log line per request
fix.text: Put a gateway between the tools and the provider. Make a new real key, keep it only in the gateway, and switch the old shared key off. Give each tool its own gateway key with a monthly budget sized from its real need: speech to text $700, the translator $400, the checker $200, the archive summariser $350, room for five weekly runs. Log every request with the key, the model, the tokens and the cost, and read the log by key: a summariser key spending at 01:00 on a Saturday is a question on day one, not a bill on day fifteen. Set the provider's own limit just above the sum of the budgets, $1,700 over $1,650, as the last fence. Give every new tool its own key, never a copy of another's. Tonight, raise the provider's limit enough to finish the month's work and ship the film; the gateway is how the next month stays seen.

limits: A budget only stops spending; it doesn't say whether the spending was right. Someone still has to read the log by key and ask why a weekly job ran on a Saturday. Budgets set by guesswork stop honest work too: $250 would have stopped the summariser's ordinary weekly runs in September.

The gateway is on every request's path and holds the keys that matter. If it is down, every tool stops at once, and if it is broken into, every key behind it is exposed. Run it somewhere reliable, guard its keys like the old shared one, and know how to run without it for a night.

Some of this exists without a gateway. Anthropic, for one, lets you set spend and rate limits per Workspace inside one organization, which gives one provider's tools separate limits. It doesn't route between providers, the keys are still pasted into each tool, and its page notes you can't set limits on the default Workspace.

explain.seniorTake: Once more than one tool talks to a model, put one door in front of the provider and give every tool its own key. The door holds the real provider keys, so they live in one guarded place instead of pasted into every machine, and a tool's key can be switched off without touching the rest. Each key gets a budget in money, and where it matters a cap on tokens or requests per minute, so a runaway job stops itself and nothing else. Every request leaves a log line with the key, the model, the tokens and the cost, so the bill splits by tool and a strange pattern has a name the first night it appears. Because everything goes through one interface, you can route by model name and add a second provider without touching the tools. Keep the provider's own limit as the outer fence, above the sum of the budgets. And treat the gateway itself as what it now is: the one program every tool depends on.

realWorld.title: LiteLLM: one endpoint for many providers
realWorld.text: LiteLLM's documentation describes its open-source gateway this way: The LiteLLM AI Gateway is a self-hosted server. It gives your applications one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for 100+ LLM providers. Self-hosted means you run it on your own machine. An endpoint is the one address the apps send to; OpenAI-compatible means apps send requests in OpenAI's format and the gateway translates for each provider.

realWorld.title: LiteLLM: keys, budgets, cost per request, routing
realWorld.text: The same page lists what the gateway does: Each key has its models, budgets, and rate limits. The gateway records the cost of each request. And for reliability: Load balancing, fallbacks, and retries move traffic between deployments when a provider has a problem.

realWorld.title: LiteLLM: a budget per key, and when it resets
realWorld.text: LiteLLM's budgets page says you can apply a budget on a key, and: After the key crosses it's max_budget, requests fail. A key's budget_duration sets when spend resets: Budget is reset at the end of specified duration. If not set, budget is never reset. Keys can also carry tpm limits (tokens per minute) and rpm limits (requests per minute). Its example error reads: Authentication Error, ExceededTokenBudget.

realWorld.title: LiteLLM: virtual keys track spend per key
realWorld.text: LiteLLM calls a gateway key a virtual key: Track Spend, and control model access via virtual keys for the proxy. Spend can be read per key, per user and per team, and the page says the feature needs a database to keep the counts: Need a postgres database.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: a spend limit for the whole organization
realWorld.text: Anthropic's rate-limits page names two kinds of limit: Spend limits set a maximum monthly cost an organization can incur for API usage, and rate limits on requests over time. Limits are set at the organization level. On a limit you set yourself: When usage reaches a spend limit you set, requests return HTTP 400 with error type invalid_request_error, with a message that begins You have reached your specified API usage limits. Raise or remove the limit to restore access sooner.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the tier's own cap is a different refusal
realWorld.text: Separately, each usage tier carries a monthly spend cap; once it is reached, usage pauses until 00:00 UTC on the first day of the next month, and requests return HTTP 429 with error type rate_limit_error and the code enforced_spend_limit_reached, with no retry-after header. Two refusals that look alike are worth telling apart in your logs.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: limits per Workspace, and new accounts start low
realWorld.text: The same page says: To protect Workspaces in your Organization from potential overuse, you can set custom spend and rate limits per Workspace, and notes You can't set limits on the default Workspace. It also says new organizations and organizations with limited usage history may start in the Evaluation tier, with limits below the standard limits.

asked: Why put a gateway in front of model providers?
How would you give each team a budget?
What does a gateway cost you?
interview.answer: Without one, every app carries a real provider key, usually the same one copied around, so the provider bills one account and can't split the spend; a single account limit stops every app at once; and changing provider means touching every app. A gateway is one program in front of all the providers. Apps call it with their own gateway key in one request format. It checks the key and its budget, reads the model name and routes to the provider that serves it, swaps in the real key that only it holds, and writes a log line with the key, model, tokens and cost. For team budgets I give each team or app its own key with a monthly budget in money, sized from a month of its own log lines, plus tokens-per-minute and requests-per-minute caps so one burst can't starve the rest; a key that reaches its budget is refused and nothing else is. I set alerts before the budget, at say 80%, and keep the provider's own limit as an outer fence above the sum of the budgets. The costs: it is on every request's path, so it needs to be reliable and I need a plan for when it is down; it holds the keys that matter, so it is guarded and its access logged; it adds a little delay; and its logs may hold sensitive prompts, so I decide what to keep. Open-source gateways such as LiteLLM, or a provider's own per-workspace limits, cover parts of this; the gateway is what covers several providers at once.

terms.def: The person who writes and times the words shown along the bottom of a film. Aoife is Lowlight's night subtitle editor.
A television channel or service that shows films. Lowlight's film was due at one at 06:00.
A program that reads text and writes text back, one likely word at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e01).
A company that runs language models and sells their use, billed by the token (a1e03). Lowlight uses one.
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads or writes and is billed by (a1e03).
One message a tool sends to the model, and the provider's word for it. Each carries a key and is billed for its tokens.
A long secret code sent with every request, like a password, that tells the provider which account to bill (a2e01 calls it an API key).
What the provider bills: it owns the keys, the limit and the usage page. Anthropic calls it an organization.
The most an account may spend in a month. Once it is reached the provider refuses every request on the account until the month resets or the limit is raised.
The most something may spend in a period. Mr Teasdale's was the whole account's $1,500; a gateway gives each key its own.
The provider's page of what the account spent, here in ten-minute bars, one line per key (a2e01).
Lowlight's tool that writes notes on every film in its archive, about $65 a run, on an old computer in the back office.
One key pasted into several tools, so they all spend on one line and one limit (a4e08).
One program between your tools and the providers: it holds the real keys, checks each tool's own key and budget, routes by model name and logs every request.
A program in front of other programs that checks, limits and routes every request on its way in (s2e09, The Front Desk).
A key the gateway hands one tool. The provider never sees it; the gateway checks it, then sends the real key on. LiteLLM calls it a virtual key.
The provider's own key. With a gateway, only the gateway holds it.
One record per request: when, which key, which model, tokens in and out, and the cost. Added up by key, it splits the bill by tool.
The gateway reading which model a request asks for and sending it to the provider that serves it (a2e08 taught routing).
The provider's own limit kept above the sum of the gateway's budgets, so it trips only if the gateway itself fails.
Make a key stop working for good, so every copy is refused at once. a2e01 calls it revoking; making a new one to replace it is rotating.
LiteLLM's setting for the most a key may spend; after that, its requests fail.
LiteLLM's setting for how often a key's spend resets, such as every month. If it is not set, the budget never resets.
Caps on tokens per minute, with rpm limits for requests per minute. LiteLLM's tpm_limit and rpm_limit set them per key.
A cap on how many requests or tokens an account or key may send in a stretch of time, such as a minute (a2e01).
Anthropic's level for an organization, which sets its rate limits and monthly spend cap. New ones may start in a lower Evaluation tier.
In Anthropic's console, a group inside one organization with its own keys; you can set it lower spend and rate limits.
The address a program sends its requests to. LiteLLM's gateway gives apps one endpoint for many providers.
Taking requests in the format OpenAI's own interface uses, so apps written for it work unchanged.
An open-source gateway for model providers, run on your own server, with keys, budgets, rate limits and cost tracking.
A code a service sends back when it refuses a request. Anthropic uses it for a spend limit you set; its tier's own cap and rate limits use 429 instead.
One part that everything depends on, so when it stops, everything stops. A gateway is one unless you run it reliably.
The course's hands-on builds. X5 is cost and speed through an LLM gateway, with caching and routing.
A program that stores records and finds them again, like a filing cabinet that answers questions. LiteLLM keeps each key's spend in one.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A lists controls such as A.5.15 access control, A.5.17 authentication information and A.8.24 use of cryptography.
An audit of a service organization's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC6.1 covers logical access to systems and data.

atWork: Look for one provider key pasted into several internal tools, and a monthly model bill nobody can split by team. It is a common pattern: a key made for one prototype gets copied into the next tool, then the next, and the usage page grows one line long. Ask four things. Where do the real provider keys live, and how many places hold a copy? Could you say last month which tool or team spent what? Could you switch one tool off without stopping the others? And what stops a job that runs wild at 01:00: its own budget, or the whole account's limit? If the answers point at a gateway, Build Night X5 is where you build one: cost and speed through an LLM gateway. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control A.5.15 (access control) and A.5.17 (authentication information) ask that access and secrets be given and managed per user or system, and A.8.24 (use of cryptography) covers how keys are managed; one shared key in four tools with no owner per use is hard to defend. If you report under SOC 2, CC6.1 asks for logical access controls over systems and data, which per-tool keys and a log line per request support. Building this in from the first tool is far cheaper than separating keys and bills before an audit.

recall.prompt: Five internal apps at your company (a support bot, a search tool, a report writer, a code reviewer and a meeting summariser) all use one provider key, copied into each app's settings. Finance asks which team spent last month's $9,000 and nobody can say. Last night all five stopped at once when the account reached its spending limit. What would you put in place?

keyIdeas.idea: A gateway in front holds the real provider key; each app gets its own key from the gateway
Each app's key has its own budget, so one app reaching it stops only that app
A log line per request with the key, model, tokens and cost, so the bill splits by app

recall.model: Put a gateway in front of the provider. Make a new real key that only the gateway holds, switch the old copied key off, and give each app a key per app from the gateway. Give each key its own budget for the month, sized from what that app really uses, so an app that runs wild stops only that app and not all five. Have the gateway write a log line for every request, with the key, the model, the tokens and the cost, so you can split the bill by app and answer finance. Keep the provider's own limit above the sum of the budgets, as the last fence.

recall.prompt: Lowlight's account had spent $1,470 by the end of 14 October and $5 more by 01:00 on the 15th. The summariser's run costs $65 over 40 minutes, from 01:00. With a $1,500 limit, when is every tool refused?
options: At about 01:15, partway through the run
recall.why: The run needs only $25 more to reach $1,500. At $65 over 40 minutes it spends $1.625 a minute, so $25 takes about 15.4 minutes: the limit fills at about 01:15. Aoife found the tools refused at 01:40, when she came back from her break.

recall.prompt: A colleague wants the gateway budget for the archive summariser at $250 a month: four weekly runs, give or take. Each run costs $65 and it runs on Sundays. What is wrong with $250, and what would you set?

keyIdeas.idea: $250 is below even four runs ($260), so the budget stops the honest weekly job
Size it for the busiest honest month: five Sundays, five runs, about $350
A nightly mistake still stops within days, on the sixth run, and the log names the key

recall.model: Four runs cost $260, so $250 is too low: it would stop the summariser's honest weekly job on the fourth Sunday, as it would have on 27 September. Size the budget for its busiest honest month, five Sundays, five runs, $325, and round up to about $350. If the schedule is ever changed to nightly by mistake, $350 still stops it within days, on the sixth run, as on 6 October, and the gateway's log line names the key, so someone asks why.

recall.prompt: At 01:40 Lowlight makes a new key, switches the old one off and pastes the new key into three tools. Why are they still refused?
options: The spending limit belongs to the account, which is already full; a new key doesn't empty it
A new key takes a day to start working
The summariser still holds the old key
The provider refuses keys made at night
recall.why: A key only tells the provider which account to bill. The limit is the account's, and the account had spent $1,500.00 of its $1,500, so every request on it is refused, whatever key it carries, until the limit is raised or the month resets.

recall.prompt: Anthropic lets you set spend and rate limits per Workspace inside one organization. Which of these does that not give you, that a gateway does?
options: Sending translation to a second provider by model name, with no change in the tools
A separate spend limit for each team
A separate tokens-per-minute limit for one team
Stopping one team's spending without stopping the others
recall.why: Workspace limits split one provider's account into parts with their own limits, so they can give each team its own spend and rate limits. They can't route a request to another provider: that needs something in front of every provider, which is what a gateway is.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The gateway works. Every tool has a key and a budget of its own, and the log names every dollar. In February Ms Mirrlees added a fifth tool, a voice-over writer, and asked Mr Corrigall for a key. He was busy, so he copied the speech tool's gateway key into it. On 20 February at 23:16 speech to text was refused, budget reached, with a series due at 06:00. The log shows the speech tool's key spending $44 a night since 9 February, twice its usual $22.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why was speech to text refused, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: Two tools share one gateway key, so they share its budget and its log line: the old problem, one level down
Give the new tool its own gateway key with its own budget
Make issuing a key quick and routine, and watch for one key used from two places

coldCase.model: The voice-over writer and speech to text share one key, so they share one $700 budget and one log line: the shared key problem again, one level down. From 9 February the key spent $44 a night instead of $22, so by the end of 19 February it had spent $660 (8 nights at $22, then 11 at $44), and $40 more filled it at 23:16 on the 20th. Give the voice-over writer its own gateway key with its own budget, sized from its first weeks, and switch the copy off. Then make issuing a key quick and routine, part of setting up every new tool, keep a list of keys with their owners, and have the gateway flag one key used from two places.
